hints: Think about what stays the same and what changes when you rearrange atoms into a different skeleton or position of a functional group.
walkthrough:
Hold the atom count fixed**
Picture building with the same set of atoms, for example all isomers of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. You have exactly five carbons, ten hydrogens and one oxygen every time. That shared count is the molecular formula part.

Rearrange the connections**
Now join those same atoms together in a different order. You could move the oxygen from the end to the middle, or branch the carbon chain. Because the connectivity is different, the structural formula is different. Same formula, different structure is structural isomerism.
Final answer: Molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae.

hints: Recall which functional group gives an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH reagent.
walkthrough:
Read the positive test**
Both A and B give an orange precipitate with 2,4-DNPH. That reagent is specific for the $\text{C=O}$ group in aldehydes and ketones. So both molecules contain a carbonyl group.
Final answer: Carbonyl group.

hints: Use Tollens result to decide which of A or B is the aldehyde and which is the ketone.
Use the negative alkaline $\text{I}_2$ result to rule out a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group, then fit a straight five carbon chain with formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Split aldehyde from ketone**
A gives a silver mirror with Tollens reagent, B shows no reaction. Only aldehydes reduce Tollens reagent, ketones do not. So A must be a straight chain aldehyde and B must be a straight chain ketone.

Use the iodoform clue**
Neither A nor B gives a yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2$. That tells you there is no $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ group present. For a five carbon aldehyde this forces $\text{CHO}$ at the end of a four carbon chain: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$.

Place the ketone carbonyl**
For B, a straight chain ketone of formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ could be pentan-2-one or pentan-3-one. Pentan-2-one contains $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ and would give a positive iodoform test, so it is ruled out. B must be pentan-3-one: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.

Final answer: A: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$ (pentanal)
B: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (pentan-3-one)

hints: Translate the three test results into functional groups: no reaction with 2,4-DNPH, decolourises $\text{Br}_2$, positive with alkaline $\text{I}_2$.
Combine a straight five carbon chain with one $\text{C=C}$ and one alcohol group that can give the iodoform result, while keeping formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.
walkthrough:
Decode each test**
No reaction with 2,4-DNPH means no aldehyde or ketone. Decolourisation of orange $\text{Br}_2\text{(aq)}$ to colourless means a $\text{C=C}$ alkene is present. Yellow precipitate with alkaline $\text{I}_2$ normally means $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ is present. Since there is no carbonyl, it must be $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$.

Build the straight chain**
You need five carbons in a row, one $\text{C=C}$ and one $\text{OH}$, with formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. Put $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}$ at one end to satisfy the iodoform test, then add $\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$ to complete the chain. That gives $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$.

Check the stereoisomerism clue**
This structure has a chiral carbon at C2 but its $\text{C=C}$ is terminal ($\text{CH=CH}_2$) so it cannot show cis-trans isomerism. That matches the statement that C shows only one type of stereoisomerism.
Final answer: C: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$ (pent-4-en-2-ol)

hints: Recall that C has a carbon with four different groups but no $\text{C=C}$ that can show cis-trans isomerism.
walkthrough:
Link structure to stereoisomerism**
In $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$ the carbon bonded to $\text{OH}$ is attached to $\text{H}$, $\text{OH}$, $\text{CH}_3$ and $\text{CH}_2\text{CH=CH}_2$. Four different groups means a chiral centre, so the molecule exists as non-superimposable mirror images. That is optical isomerism.
Final answer: Optical isomerism.

hints: Look at the ring in Fig. 5.1 where a $\text{C=O}$ is joined through an $\text{O}$ bridge in the same molecule.
walkthrough:
Spot the COO link**
In E the carbonyl carbon $\text{C=O}$ is directly bonded to a ring oxygen $\text{O}$. That $\text{COO}$ arrangement inside a ring is an ester group, sometimes called a lactone.
Final answer: Ester.

hints: Think about the reaction type where two groups join and a small molecule such as water is lost.
walkthrough:
Follow the water**
D forms E plus water. Joining parts of the same molecule with loss of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ is the classic signature of a condensation reaction, here intramolecular esterification.
Final answer: Condensation.

hints: Work backwards from the cyclic ester E by opening the ring at the $\text{C-O}$ single bond and adding back the atoms of water.
walkthrough:
Open the lactone**
Imagine hydrolysing the ester bond in the five membered ring. The $\text{C=O}$ side becomes a carboxylic acid $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ and the $\text{O}$ side becomes an alcohol $\text{OH}$. Counting round the ring gives a straight chain: $\text{HOCH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, which is 4-hydroxypentanoic acid.
Final answer: $\text{HOCH(CH}_3\text{)CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{C(=O)OH}$ (4-hydroxypentanoic acid)

hints: List the bonds present in D but absent in E, focusing on $\text{O-H}$ groups above $1500 \text{cm}^{-1}$.
Compare the $\text{C=O}$ absorption ranges for an ester (1710-1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$) and a carboxyl group (1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$) using Table 5.3.
walkthrough:
Compare the functional groups**
E is only an ester, so above $1500 \text{cm}^{-1}$ it shows mainly $\text{C-H}$ around 2850-2950 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and ester $\text{C=O}$ around 1710-1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. D is a hydroxy carboxylic acid, so it has two extra $\text{O-H}$ types plus a carboxylic $\text{C=O}$.

Predict the new O-H bands in D**
D will show a very broad $\text{O-H}$ band for the carboxyl group at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ and a broad $\text{O-H}$ band for the alcohol at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Neither appears in the spectrum of E in Fig. 5.2, which is flat in those regions except for $\text{C-H}$.

Predict the C=O shift**
The $\text{C=O}$ stretch moves slightly: carboxylic acid in D absorbs at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, while the cyclic ester in E absorbs at 1710-1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$. Quoting any two distinct differences with bond, group and wavenumber range earns full credit.

Final answer: Any two of:
D shows broad $\text{O-H}$ (carboxyl) absorption at 2500-3000 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, absent in E.
D shows $\text{O-H}$ (hydroxy, alcohol) absorption at 3200-3600 $\text{cm}^{-1}$, absent in E.
D shows $\text{C=O}$ (carboxyl) at 1670-1740 $\text{cm}^{-1}$ whereas E shows $\text{C=O}$ (ester) at 1710-1750 $\text{cm}^{-1}$.
